subject: design-technology
title: Modelling
final_note: You worked through the key terms in Modelling.

concepts.def: A representation of a design idea - physical, graphical or virtual - used to explore, test and communicate the design before full production.
Quick, informal drawings used early in designing to generate, explore and record many ideas rapidly and at very low cost.
A formal working drawing showing accurate front, side and plan views with dimensions, so that a product can be manufactured correctly.
Testing a CAD model in software, for example simulating stresses, fit or movement, before any physical part is manufactured.
A quick model, often full-scale and in cheap materials such as foam or card, used to assess the size, form and ergonomics of a design.
A working model close to the final product, used to test function, manufacturing methods and user response before committing to production.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Modelling — a core area of Design Technology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Modelling brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Modelling.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: An orthographic projection is used to:
options: Show accurate dimensioned views so the product can be manufactured
Brainstorm rough initial concepts
Test a product with focus groups
Advertise the finished product

mcqs.q: A full-size foam model made to check how a handle fits the hand is called a:
options: Prototype
Mock-up
Orthographic drawing
Production die

mcqs.q: The key difference between a mock-up and a prototype is that a prototype:
options: Is always smaller than the real product
Is made before any sketching happens
Actually works, so function can be tested, not just form
Never uses real materials

mcqs.q: A major advantage of virtual prototyping is that it:
options: Eliminates all need for physical testing forever
Is only available to very large companies
Makes the final product weigh less
Finds problems by simulation before money is spent on physical parts

mcqs.q: Is a prototype the same as the final product?
options: Yes - prototypes are simply early units sold to customers.
Yes - physical testing is only done for marketing photos.
No - a prototype is a test version used to prove function and reveal problems; materials, finish and manufacturing method may still change before production.
Yes - once a prototype exists, the design is finished.

mcqs.q: Do sketches need to be neat and accurate to be useful?
options: Yes - a sketch is worthless unless drawn to scale with a ruler.
Yes - prototypes are simply early units sold to customers.
Yes - designers only sketch after the design is finalised.
No - early sketches are thinking tools; speed and quantity of ideas matter more than neatness, and accuracy comes later in formal working drawings.

mcqs.q: If a CAD simulation says a design is strong enough, is physical testing unnecessary?
options: Yes - designers only sketch after the design is finalised.
No - simulations rely on simplified assumptions about materials and loads; physical testing is still needed to validate the model against reality.
Yes - physical testing is only done for marketing photos.
Yes - computer simulation results are always exactly right.
